content: The references provided are a collection of studies, reviews, and guidelines addressing various aspects of public health, particularly focusing on tuberculosis (TB), HIV, viral hepatitis, and related comorbidities. 1. Edge S, Leung J, Grebely J, Vickerman P, et al. conducted a systematic review to determine the global prevalence of injecting drug use, as well as the sociodemographic characteristics and prevalence of HIV, HBV, and HCV among people who inject drugs. This study provides critical insights into the burden of infectious diseases in this population. (Lancet Glob Health, 2017) 2. Dolan K, Wirtz AL, Moazen B, Ndeffo-Mbah M, Galvani A, Kinner SA, et al. explored the global burden of HIV, viral hepatitis, and tuberculosis among prisoners and detainees. Their findings highlight the disproportionate impact of these diseases in incarcerated populations. (Lancet, 2016) 3. Citro B, Soltan V, Malar J, Katlholo T, Smyth C, Sari AH, et al. analyzed the Stop TB Partnership’s community, rights, and gender tuberculosis assessment to advocate for a rights-based, people-centered, and gender-transformative TB response. (Health Hum Rights, 2021) 4. Lan CW, Lin C, Thanh DC, Li L. examined the impact of drug-related stigma on access to care among people who inject drugs in Vietnam, emphasizing the barriers to healthcare access in this vulnerable group. (Drug Alcohol Rev, 2018) 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring provide evidence-based recommendations for a public health approach to HIV management. (Geneva: WHO, 2021) 6. Getahun H, Gunneberg C, Sculier D, Verster A, Raviglione M. reviewed the intersection of tuberculosis and HIV in people who inject drugs, emphasizing the need for integrated TB, HIV, prison, and harm reduction services. (Curr Opin HIV AIDS, 2012) 7. Duko B, Bedaso A, Ayano G. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the prevalence of depression among patients with tuberculosis, highlighting the mental health burden in this population. (Ann Gen Psychiatry, 2020) 8. The WHO website provides resources and information on people who inject drugs, focusing on their health needs and the importance of harm reduction strategies. (Accessed March 2022) 9. The WHO and United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime published revised international standards for the treatment of drug use disorders, incorporating field-testing results to improve care delivery. (Geneva: WHO, 2020) 10. WHO guidelines on alternatives to conviction or punishment for people with drug use disorders in contact with the criminal justice system emphasize treatment and care over punitive measures. (Accessed March 2022) 11. WHO’s report on health, rights, and drugs advocates for harm reduction, decriminalization, and zero discrimination for people who use drugs, aiming to improve health outcomes and reduce stigma. (Accessed March 2022) 12. Alene KA, Clements ACA, McBryde ES, Jaramillo E, Lönnroth K, Shaweno D, et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the impact of mental health disorders, social stressors, and health-related quality of life in patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. (J Infect, 2018) 13. Lee GE, Scuffell J, Galea JT, Shin SS, Magill E, Jaramillo E, et al. investigated the impact of mental disorders on active tuberculosis treatment outcomes, providing evidence for the integration of mental health services in TB care. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2020) 14. Pasha A, Siddiqui H, Ali S, Brooks MB, Maqbool NR, Khan AJ. evaluated the integration of mental health services within tuberculosis treatment facilities, demonstrating the benefits of a holistic approach to care. (Medicine Access @ Point of Care, 2021) 15. WHO’s consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, care, and support provide comprehensive recommendations for managing TB patients, including those with comorbidities. (Geneva: WHO, 2022) 16. WHO’s global progress report on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (2021) outlines accountability measures and actions for achieving global health sector strategy goals. (Geneva: WHO, 2021) 17. Feleke BE, Feleke TE, Adane WG, Girma A. conducted a prospective cohort study to assess the impacts of hepatitis B and C co-infection on tuberculosis outcomes, emphasizing the need for integrated care. (Virol J, 2020) 18. Bushnell G, Stennis NL, Drobnik AM, Proops DC, Ahuja SD, Bornschlegel K, et al. analyzed TB treatment outcomes in patients with viral hepatitis in New York City, highlighting the challenges of managing co-infections. (Epidemiol Infect, 2015) 19. WHO guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing provide evidence-based recommendations for improving diagnosis and linkage to care. (Geneva: WHO, 2017) 20. WHO’s guidelines on integrating TB and HIV services within a comprehensive care package for people who inject drugs emphasize the importance of collaborative care models. (Geneva: WHO, 2016) 21. WHO’s evidence-to-decision framework supports the management of latent tuberculosis infection, providing a structured approach to decision-making. (Accessed March 2022) 22. WHO’s people-centered framework for tuberculosis program planning and prioritization offers a user guide for implementing patient-focused strategies. (Geneva: WHO, 2019) 23. WHO’s multisectoral accountability framework aims to accelerate progress toward ending tuberculosis by 2030, emphasizing the importance of cross-sector collaboration. (Geneva: WHO, 2019) 24. Horter S, Daftary A, Keam T, Bernays S, Bhanushali K, Chavan D, et al. explored the implementation of person-centered care in tuberculosis management, advocating for patient-focused approaches. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2021) 25. Odone A, Roberts B, Dara M, van den Boom M, Kluge H, McKee M. reviewed models of care for tuberculosis that prioritize peopleand patient-centered approaches, highlighting best practices. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2018) 26. Goodwin N. discussed the role of local communities in delivering people-centered care, emphasizing the importance of integration and community engagement. (Int J Integr Care, 2014) 27. WHO’s ethics guidance for implementing the End TB strategy provides a framework for addressing ethical challenges in tuberculosis care. (Geneva: WHO, 2017) 28. Lönnroth K, Jaramillo E, Williams BG, Dye C, Raviglione M. examined the role of risk factors and social determinants in driving tuberculosis epidemics, emphasizing the need for comprehensive interventions. (Soc Sci Med, 2009) 29. Bukhman G, Mocumbi AO, Atun R, Becker AE, Bhutta Z, Binagwaho A, et al. highlighted the Lancet NCDI Poverty Commission’s efforts to bridge gaps in universal health coverage for the poorest populations. (Lancet, 2020) 30. Watkins DA, Jamison DT, Mills T, Atun T, Danforth K, Glassman A, et al. discussed the role of universal health coverage and essential care packages in improving health and reducing poverty. (Disease Control Priorities, 3rd ed., 2017) 31. WHO’s TB Knowledge Sharing Platform provides resources for healthcare professionals to enhance tuberculosis care and management. (Accessed March 2022) 32. The United Nations Common Position on Ending HIV, TB, and Viral Hepatitis emphasizes intersectoral collaboration to address these global health challenges. (Accessed March 2022) 33. Eang MT, Vun MC, Eam KK, Sovannarith S, Sopheap S, Bora N, et al. described the multi-step process of building TB/HIV collaboration in Cambodia, highlighting lessons learned. (Health Res Policy Syst, 2012) 34. Okot-Chono R, Mugisha F, Adatu F, Madraa E, Dlodo R, Fujiwara P. identified health system barriers affecting the implementation of collaborative TB-HIV services in Uganda. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2009) 35. WHO’s handbook on strategizing national health in the 21st century provides guidance for effective health system planning and implementation. (Geneva: WHO, 2016) 36. Cords O, Martinez L, Warren JL, O’Marr JM, Walter KS, Cohen T, et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the incidence and prevalence of tuberculosis in incarcerated populations, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. (Lancet Public Health, 2021) 37. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control and WHO Regional Office for Europe published a report on tuberculosis surveillance and monitoring in Europe, providing valuable data for public health planning. (Geneva: WHO, 2020) 38. Altice FL, Azbel L, Stone J, Brooks-Pollock E, Smyrnov P, Dvoriak S, et al. described the high-risk environment of incarceration in perpetuating the transmission of HIV, hepatitis C, and tuberculosis in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. (Lancet, 2016) 39. The Pompidou Group’s country profile on Moldova provides an overview of the drug situation and policy, emphasizing the need for evidence-based interventions. (Accessed March 2022) 40. WHO’s Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) manual offers a monitoring system for evaluating service delivery in healthcare settings. (Geneva: WHO, 2016) 41. Castellanos-Joya M, Delgado-Sánchez G, Ferreyra-Reyes L, Cruz-Hervert P, Ferreira-Guerrero E, Ortiz-Solís G, et al. reported on the implementation of a pilot model for bidirectional screening and joint management of tuberculosis and diabetes in Mexico. (PLoS One, 2014) 42. Mexico’s official guidelines for tuberculosis prevention and control provide a framework for national TB management strategies. (Accessed March 2022) 43. WHO’s initiative on addressing the burden of tuberculosis and non-communicable diseases in vulnerable populations emphasizes the importance of integrated care. (Accessed March 2022) 44. The Declaration of Astana reaffirmed global commitment to primary healthcare as a foundation for achieving universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. (Geneva: WHO, 2018) 45. WHO’s compendium of data and evidence-related tools supports tuberculosis program planning and implementation, providing resources for evidence-based decision-making. (Geneva: WHO, 2021) 46. Gilbert JA, Shenoi SV, Moll AP, Friedland GH, Paltiel AD, Galvani AP. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of community-based TB/HIV screening and linkage to care in rural South Africa, demonstrating the value of decentralized care models. (PLoS One, 2016) 47. Williams AO, Makinde OA, Ojo M. compared community-based management with traditional hospitalization for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis, highlighting the benefits of decentralized care. (Glob Health Res Policy, 2016) 48. WHO’s Regional Office for Europe assessed the accessibility and integration of HIV, TB, and harm reduction services for people who inject drugs in Portugal, providing recommendations for service improvement. (Accessed March 2022) 49. Naher N, Balabanova D, Hutchinson E, Marten R, Hoque R, Tune SNBK, et al. reviewed the effectiveness of social accountability approaches in improving health outcomes in lowand middle-income countries. (Health Policy Plan, 2020) 50. Chifundo K. shared experiences from Malawi on the best models of TB/HIV service delivery, emphasizing the importance of integrated care. (AIDS 2010 Conference) 51. De Foo C, Shrestha P, Wang L, Du Q, García-Basteiro AL, Abdullah AS, et al. conducted a systematic review on integrating tuberculosis and non-communicable disease care in lowand middle-income countries, highlighting the benefits of comprehensive care. (PLoS Med, 2022) 52. Legido-Quigley H, Montgomery CM, Khan P, Atun R, Fakoya A, Getahun H, et al. reviewed the integration of tuberculosis and HIV services in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing the need for collaborative care models. (Trop Med Int Health, 2013) 53. WHO’s case study on China highlights the use of multidisciplinary teams and integrated service delivery across levels of care to improve health outcomes. (Geneva: WHO, 2018) 54. WHO’s guidelines on tuberculosis infection prevention and control provide updated recommendations for reducing TB transmission in healthcare and community settings. (Geneva: WHO, 2019) 55. WHO’s compendium of good practices in the health sector response to viral hepatitis in the European Region provides examples of successful interventions. (Copenhagen: WHO, 2020) 56. WHO’s report on integrated screening for infectious diseases in Georgia highlights the success of collaborative approaches to disease management. (Accessed March 2022) 57. Salifu RS, Hlongwana KW. explored healthcare workers’ perspectives on barriers and facilitators to bidirectional screening of tuberculosis and diabetes in Ghana, providing insights for improving care delivery. (PLoS One, 2020) 58. Lovero KL, Lammie SL, van Zyl A, Paul SN, Ngwepe P, Mootz JJ, et al. evaluated the integration of mental healthcare into tuberculosis and maternal-child healthcare services in South Africa, demonstrating the feasibility and benefits of integrated care. (BMC Health Serv Res, 2019) 59. Tola HH, Shojaeizadeh D, Tol A, Garmaroudi G, Yekaninejad MS, Kebede A, et al. conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial in Ethiopia to assess the impact of psychological and educational interventions on tuberculosis treatment adherence. (PLoS One, 2016) 60. Majumdar A, Wilkinson E, Rinu PK, Maung TM, Bachani D, Punia JS, et al. conducted a mixed-methods study in North India to evaluate the effectiveness of tuberculosis-diabetes screening programs. (Public Health Action, 2019) 61. Avoka VA, Osei E. evaluated TB/HIV collaborative activities in Ghana, providing insights into the effectiveness of integrated care models. (Tuberc Res Treat, 2020) 62. Zvolska K, Pankova A, Nohavova I, Huque R, Elsey H, Boeckmann M, et al. reviewed facilitators and barriers to smoking cessation and tobacco-dependence treatment in tuberculosis patients in lowand middle-income countries. (Tob Induc Dis, 2020) 63. Degefa MG, Bezabih AM, Kahsay ZH, Belachew AB. explored barriers and facilitators of nutrition assessment, counseling, and support for tuberculosis patients, emphasizing the importance of addressing nutritional needs. (BMC Nutr, 2021) 64. Gebremariam MK, Bjune GA, Frich JC. conducted a qualitative study on barriers and facilitators of adherence to tuberculosis treatment in patients on concomitant TB and HIV treatment, providing insights for improving adherence. (BMC Public Health, 2010) 65. Boeckmann M, Warsi S, Noor M, Dogar O, Mustagfira EH, Firoze F, et al. explored healthcare worker and patient views on implementing smoking cessation in routine tuberculosis care, highlighting the challenges and opportunities. (NPJ Prim Care Respir Med, 2019) 66. Sommerland N, Wouters E, Mitchell EMH, Ngicho M, Redwood L, Masquillier C, et al. conducted a systematic review of evidence-based interventions to reduce tuberculosis stigma, providing recommendations for stigma reduction strategies. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2017) 67. Contreras CC, Millones AK, Santa Cruz J, Aguilar M, Clendenes M, Toranzo M, et al. described a comprehensive programmatic approach to addressing the medical and socio-economic needs of tuberculosis patients, emphasizing the importance of holistic care. (Trop Med Int Health)
